utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked for the witness to be kept out for a few minutes, because there are a couple of matters that I want to raise arising from yesterday's ruling on admissibility, and I think it's better that they be dealt with now rather than later. In the result, I'm going to be inviting the Court to consider, at this stage, whether in light of its ruling, it should now be considering itself making preparations for calling other witnesses, that is, the Court should be calling witnesses. Secondly, I am going to invite the Court to correct what may now be, in the mind of the witness, as a reflection on his evidence by the Chamber, something that would be incorrect, I would suspect, as a reflection by the Chamber of his evidence, and I would like it to be corrected. I'll take a couple of minutes to explain our concerns, although I expect many of them will be readily understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I'm sorry to interrupt, but this really is a matter for the Trial Chamber. We have made a ruling. I don't see that the witness is going to be in any way affected by our ruling, and I don't really see what matters arise from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope the Court will give me a chance to develop this. This is an important matter, and it may be that one of its problems yesterday is that it was dealt with some speed and in a way that made the best resolution of the problem not immediately available. The problem, really, is this -- not the problem, but the general issue is this: Hearsay evidence is admissible in this Tribunal. The Tadic rules, we've been applying, but we've been applying them in shorthand. Hearsay is admissible for a number of reasons particular to this Tribunal. If hearsay evidence is excluded at an early stage rather than admitted subject to later evaluation, a real problem arises if I'm then in a position to produce evidence that supports that which was the underlying evidence excluded or, indeed, if the evidence generally points to that conclusion. So in the immediate case, which is now already the subject of a ruling, but just in the immediate case, if I were to produce and able to produce later evidence to the same effect, exclusion of this evidence might mean that it could then not be of value in relation to consideration of the later evidence. So that's an important point, and that's why, as a matter of general principle, we will be inviting you, and this problem is going to recur, which is why I come to grips with it straightaway, we will invite you still to be, in general, admitting evidence and evaluating it later when all the evidence is in. Of course, yesterday's evidence, in part, was first-hand hearsay because the witness saw the order. Sorry, the witness spoke of the person who saw the order. So that's a matter of concern to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's second-hand hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the document is itself hearsay, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There it is. Now, yesterday I made the point, and this is, I think, where it was my error for not making the point clearly enough and, indeed, drawing some concern from Your Honour, I made the point that this is the best evidence that we are able to present to you as another of the reasons why hearsay is admissible. The point was made, well, "You're saying because cases are difficult, you want different rules to apply," and I rejected that firmly and I reject it today. But the reality in this category of case tried by this Tribunal is that evidence of this type will frequently be the best that we can make available, because, and we know the position on the ground, we don't have access. We, the Prosecution, don't have access to the witnesses who could provide better evidence. Now, if we take, for example, yesterday's evidence, there are, I think, some four witnesses who might be able to support what the witness himself said. Three of those, by reason of where they live and their loyalties, are almost certainly simply not available. I'm rechecking what enquires we've made of them, but they are not available to us, the Prosecutor. The fourth one is available and is still in the process of being contacted again; recently not available to us, but we forecast she will be. Now, when the Chamber is presented with an important issue, although this isn't a critical issue, it's a very important issue for which the best evidence that we can provide is the evidence we offered yesterday. If the Chamber is minded to say that evidence isn't going to be enough and it knows that the Prosecution can't get at the better evidence because of where they live and of their loyalties, then, in our very respectful submission, if the Chamber is going to be excluding evidence at that stage and of that category, then the Chamber could very usefully say to itself, "Well, if the Chamber requires these witnesses, who can give a better level of evidence, to attend," and the writ of the Chamber is something that is going to be difficult for any of the relevant authorities in this territory to refuse, why then the Chamber should case by case be considering that and, although it may be inconvenient and may take some time, taking the appropriate steps. The reason I mention it now is because if I'm right and that's something that the Chamber should be considering, then either via me or itself, the Chamber should be checking on the details of the witnesses through the instant witness and, indeed, in case it's material, as it might be in a case like this, checking with the witness whether he has any interest or attitude himself on the topic, for, of course, on the witness's account, these are people who saved his life, and no doubt he believes that. But in any event, that's issue number 1, and on the assumption that the Chamber is not departing in any way from the Tadic ruling so that there's no question of a new jurisprudential approach to be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me make this point: We, as I said, were not in that case making a ruling as to general principle. It is true that I think on two occasions now, we have rejected second-hand hearsay about documents. The argument you seem to be putting forward is the argument which I rejected yesterday, which is that somehow different rules should apply because this is a difficult case to prove. The fact is that we shall go on applying, on a case-by-case basis, Rule 89, and if we come to the conclusion that evidence does not have sufficient probative value and it is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, we will exclude the evidence. The fact that the Prosecution find it a difficult case, I'm afraid, is not a relevant matter. As for the necessity or the possibility of the Court calling witnesses, that is a matter which, in due course, we may have to consider, if we are invited to do so. But we would have to consider all the circumstances and the length of the trial and various other matters, of course. But at this stage, unless we're invited to make a ruling, I don't propose to do so. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a couple of more things to say, and I understand that the Court will be watching the clock. But when matters of importance are raised, I'm not going to pepper my addresses with that phrase, "with great respect," because all too often judges interpret it the reverse way. We have great respect for the Chamber. We understand your difficulties. But when there are important issues to raise, I'm afraid to say time simply has to be available to deal with them. This is an important issue and it's going to recur. Dealing with the two points Your Honour raises, I repeat what I summarised yesterday and have said this morning. We aren't in any way inviting different rules to apply to difficult cases. That's not our function. The only different approach I made is one I hope I've articulated clearly; namely, that by keeping evidence open, subject to later evaluation, the Court will not find itself in the extremely embarrassing position of saying, "Well, we've now got some admissible evidence on this topic, but we've already ruled out that which could have supported it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you inviting us then to reconsider our ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I'm not, because that ruling has been made. The second point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, there was a ruling, indeed, which was made, and you're saying that you have difficulties in the field that we know, because after all, we are informed of the difficulties that the Prosecution has in the field for several reasons. You're saying that there may be a witness or a couple of witnesses who could confirm what was said yesterday on the basis of rumours, and you're saying that the Chamber could call them. That is an initiative that remains open, and that doesn't prevent you from coming back on the substance of the problem. So it's up to you to make that proposal, and it's up to the Chamber to decide at a given time to call in this or that witness whom you feel is important for us to hear. There was a decision yesterday, but if there are other pieces of evidence, other evidence to be given, this can be had through an initiative of the Chamber itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought that I had already effectively made the invitation to Your Honours that you should consider calling the witnesses, one of whom certainly has been named, the biology teacher, and there are two others, the people who took him on the moment of his exchange, who can be approached. The second point that answers both His Honour Judge May's and His Honour Judge Bennouna's general concerns is at least in part this: If the Chamber decides to call a witness on an important issue like this, because we can't call the witness, the witness would presumably be called and available for cross-examination by either side, in the way that is so frequently done in inquiries and hearings of that sort. It would be necessary for me to be able to cross-examine that witness on the basis of things he had said on another occasion to another witness, so that it would be necessary for the evidence of what was said to be available as evidence, without prejudice to the fact that the Tribunal had ruled it inadmissible in itself as hearsay. So that's another problem, and we can't keep calling, for example, this witness back to give evidence again. I'm looking forward to resolution of these problems, and I have in mind, let me say straightaway, not a partisan approach; this is an inquiry of a fact-finding Tribunal, your rules say that, where we are here to help you. Now, this is not -- and this comes to my last point, my second point and my last point -- about the witness himself. This is an important issue. He's raised it. He raised it in his first signed statement in detail: Namely, why was he released when he had taken, apparently, no steps himself, raised no initiative to do so? It's an important issue. He raises the issue as against the first defendant, and it's for resolution. When Your Honour says, "Well, the Prosecution find it difficult, and they want different rules," that's not the case. Yes, it's difficult. I'm seeking to identify the means to get the best, safest, long-term resolution, and that's the reason I'm raising it. And finally, as to the witness himself, this is my concern: He's a man who's been here four times as a witness, five times at least, as a visitor, because he wasn't called once, and the Court will see his demeanour, and I know much of what he feels about this process of coming back and back. He heard the ruling yesterday which spoke of the evidence being unreliable. Now, I don't know -- because I haven't spoken to him -- I don't know how he interprets that. He's an intelligent man. Indeed, I have some difficulties, in reading the Tadic ruling, in deciding whether the unreliability is supposed to attach to the witness in court or to the material to which he refers, or the other witness, or both. I assume, but I haven't seen any authority, that it means both. But in his mind, it may be that he will be concluding that this Tribunal, before he's been asked any question by the Defence, is saying that there is something in what he has said which is unreliable. I doubt whether that could conceivably be the case, for there is no question of his reliability having been challenged, either by the Defence or, indeed, by the Chamber, and he has yet to be cross-examined. That will start very soon, and it would be, in my submission, very unfortunate if a witness who has helped this Tribunal generally on four occasions, and is man of integrity and education, it would be extremely unfortunate if he were to have to start the hearing today with a provisional ruling of unreliability in his ears. He may not interpret it like that; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'd like to find out whether the Prosecution has endeavoured to get these other witnesses who you say might be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, my understanding -- and I'm having it checked -- is that three of them fall within a category where the mechanisms by which we operate would not be effective in their case, not possible. The fourth has been seen, has not been asked specifically about this issue, has recently been approached but is temporarily not available to us, but it is intended to see her soon, so that she will be approached. But the other three -- and I can confirm this, I hope, by lunchtime -- have not been approached because they fall in that general category of witnesses who are essentially unavailable to us. And that's the problem, a problem for resolution not by changing the rules -- and, indeed, if Your Honours remember the way I dealt with Mr. Sayers' first objection on the hearsay point, my first hearing before this Tribunal, I was probably less enthusiastic for hearsay than others in the court and less enthusiastic than I should have been. Those were my instincts. I have no desire to change the rules, and I have no desire to see convictions recorded other than where the material is fully there to justify the conclusion, but I am concerned that the particular difficulties of this Tribunal must be reflected at all stages. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have listened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we are much further. You complain of our ruling. We have given you the reasons for it. You say it will lead to difficulties. We understand that. You now want us to turn to the witness. What do you want us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, I don't complain of your ruling; I've dealt with it, but I certainly don't complain of it. Second, what I would like you to do with the witness, apart from to take initiatives in relation to calling witnesses if you so judge that's sensible, what I'd like you to do with the witness, please, is to check that what you said about unreliability is not taken as a reflection in any way on what he has said, because as I understood your ruling, that related to the material of which he was speaking and its intrinsic unreliability at second remove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, why don't you -- you are examining the witness; why don't you deal with the matter, rather than inviting the Court to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can explain that it was a ruling of the Court and not a reflection upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do just that. Thank you very much. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, before I return to the limited number of questions I have to ask you this morning, can I just explain something to you, with the leave of the Chamber. Yesterday you had to sit through a ruling, or some argument about evidence and a ruling. In the course of that ruling there was some reference to reliability or unreliability, and I'm in the position to tell you that that word, "unreliability," in no way reflected adversely on you or what you had told the Chamber. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other questions about your exchange, I think, and I may have asked this yesterday, but I think not: Had you taken any initiative yourself to effect your exchange in the way you described?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, but I was surprised that Dr. Bruno Buzuk offered --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need; you had taken no initiatives yourself. The exchange, I think, was effected in ambulances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that in any way a standard way of effecting exchanges, or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, whose idea was it that you should go in an ambulance? Just the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that an HVO soldier, a military policeman, came to fetch me, and he took me to the operations clinic, and he told me on the way that he was sent by Darko Kraljevic, that Darko Kraljevic had sent him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the name --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For me to work in the outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the soldier? If you don't, just say no.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Dragan Calic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Following your exchange, in what town did you live?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I lived with relatives, or rather with my sister, in Zenica, and I worked in the village of Poculica and for a part in Zenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One question on, really, topic 17: Were you thereafter able to engage in any political activity, and in a sentence, if so, what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, before coming to topic 17, I should like to have a clarification from the witness on the circumstances of that exchange, of his departure. I should like to know if the witness himself expressed the desire to leave, the will to leave, before the exchange took place. Did he express to any authority the wish or the will to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please, Dr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said yesterday that this HVO soldier, Trpimir Vujica, informed me on a Friday, I think it was the 16th of May, that they, the soldiers who were providing security for the health clinic in Vitez, had been given orders by Dario Kordic that the next time I go --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, don't worry about this, Dr. Mujezinovic; that's something that we don't need to have repeated. But within the overall evidence that you could give, can you just deal with Judge Bennouna's question: Namely, had you expressed to any authority the wish or the will to leave? It may be it's a question you can answer by yes or no; if the answer is yes, you must say to which authority.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that satisfies Your Honour's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So the witness never expressed the will to leave. Before the 16th of May, was there a threat to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid here, Your Honour, we are bound by the Court's ruling, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, before, before the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Before the 16th of May. I'm saying, before the 16th of May, was he threatened? Did he receive any threats to his life, or any other threat? It's important for us to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, specifically relating to the period before the 16th of May, any threats to your life? If so, summarise it or them.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On one occasion, there was just a verbal threat by an HVO soldier whose name was Stipo Ramljak. But neither I nor my family, throughout that period, didn't have absolutely any problems while I was working in Vitez. We really didn't have any problems or threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So following your exchange, while you were with relations, were you able to engage in any, and if so, what, political activity? Just in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I was exchanged, I had a telephone contact with my wife, because after my departure my family was mistreated. HVO soldiers would break into the apartment during the night and threaten them. One night they tried to rape my wife, and this was prevented by the civilian HVO police who were called in by Croat neighbours. I refused to engage in any politics, because I was supposed to go again to participate in negotiations organised by UNPROFOR which was stationed in Nova Bila. UNPROFOR soldiers went to fetch my family twice to bring them out of Vitez. They did not succeed. On one occasion, it was the International Red Cross that made an attempt but failed, because my family was prohibited from leaving. My family was exchanged, and Edib Zlotrg, as a liaison officer of the 3rd Corps, was in charge. Through his mediation and mine, I called up some Croats in Vitez and pleaded with them to help my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your family get exchanged; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you or they ever able to take any property out of your flat, your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I left Vitez with my doctor's bag, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am so sorry. After the exchange of your family, were you able to engage in politics or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I continued to work as a doctor and as the president of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you questions about that, but you are able to answer the Defence questions about that, if they want to know. Topic 16. The defendant Dario Kordic, you've made one or two references to him. Over what period of time did you see him in the flesh, I mean see him personally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I met Dario Kordic twice briefly, once as a member of the crisis staff of the municipality and the second time when Busovaca and Vitez were shelled, and a third time in August, when an HVO brigade was lined up at the football stadium in Vitez. I stayed there briefly because I had to intervene. There was an HVO soldier in the line. I attended, twice, regional meetings in Busovaca and Vitez, and I listened to what Dario Kordic was saying. After that, I received information, as president of the war presidency, and the speeches of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble you with that. The period of time in total then that you saw him, starting the earliest time, roughly when?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was in March, when I was assigned the duty of forming a wartime medical service in Vitez. My deputy was a Croat, Dr. Bruno Buzuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you saw the defendant, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform, a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it always a military uniform or was he ever in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never saw Dario Kordic in other clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the uniform bear any patch or other indication of unit or organisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It bore the customary HVO insignia, and on his cap, he also had the patch, the usual insignia. I never saw him with any insignia of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he alone or was he accompanied when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first time I met him at the Tisa Hotel, as he was attending a meeting, and he went out for a minute or two. Dr. Bruno Buzuk said why we had come and introduced me. He heard us out, went back to the office, wrote out a piece of paper, and said, "Go to Grude --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stop you again. Was Dario Kordic accompanied when you saw him? Did he have other people with him? If so, describe them.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I saw him in Vitez after the shelling of Busovaca, he came under military escort. The same applies to Travnik. And another time at a larger meeting in Busovaca, I came earlier, I don't know whether he had an escort. He entered the hall where the meeting was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was he addressed by those with whom he was associating or who were with him? What title or term did they use when speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I listened on the local media when Dario Kordic was introduced as the first Croat of Central Bosnia, as a colonel, as a deputy president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how did people, for example, the military escort, if you ever heard them addressing him, how did they address him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention to that. I just remember hearing it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I want.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And these people in Vitez would say that he was a colonel and deputy president of Herceg-Bosna. That is how he was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have three questions about names, and that's all. You may have trouble with this, but I haven't checked on the transcript. Just tell us, the military police who took you to the cinema on the 19th of April, can you give us their name or names?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One name was Anto Kovac, known as Zabac, and the other was Ratko Nuk. I didn't know Ratko Nuk as well as I knew Anto Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A second question about names. Did you, at some stage in the course of events you've told us about, examine a man called Senad Petak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I examined him around the 21st of May. Actually, I've testified about that. That is, that was the first incident, a soldier arrested by the HVO police, he and another man called Trako. This one, Senad, was terribly beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Faud Zeco?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you examine that man?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Faud Zeco?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Faud Zeco?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's a veterinary surgeon in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you spoke of him yesterday. Did you examine him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He had a nose injury. I think it was towards the end of October when he called me and asked me whether his nose had been broken. He said that he was met by HVO soldiers in the village of Hranska and that they beat him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need. Thank you very much. Will you wait, then, because you'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, are you going to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Mr. President, by your leave. We would start with the Defence counsel of the second defendant first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm an attorney from Rijeka and representing Mario Cerkez, together with Colleague Mikulicic. I shall try and be brief, and I appeal to you for cooperation, and I hope we will understand one another well. Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, first, are you a religious man? Do you practice your religion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am a believer, but I do not regularly go to the mosque. I go twice a year for the Bajram holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before 1990, were you, to the greater or lesser degree, a religious man? Has your attitude towards religion changed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the changes that occurred in 1991 did not change your habits regarding your faith?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can that be said generally for a broader circle of intellectuals or your friends that you socialised with in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me try and rephrase the question. Could you tell us whether, among your friends and acquaintances within the circle you moved in, did their attitude towards religion change when a change of government occurred?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true if I were to say that people, as a rule, demonstrated their religious feelings more powerfully than before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my view, that was nothing more than an abuse of religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you say "abuse of religion," do you mean all religions that were practised in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you believe that this abuse of religion was present among Catholics, Orthodox and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were very few Orthodox Christians in our surroundings, but among the Muslims and Croats, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, Dr. Mujezinovic, please, in 1990, at the time of multi-party development, that is, just before the collapse of Yugoslavia, whose citizen were you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is, nationality.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was a citizen of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the actual legal status of citizenship? What did it mean to be a citizen of the SFRY in those days?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It meant that I was a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that according to the regulations in force at the time, citizens in Yugoslavia first had their Republican citizenship from which the citizenship of the SFRY was derived?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, because in my ID card, I always wrote down that I was a citizen of the SFRY. Then there was also the republic you belonged to, and you would fill in that column, too, in official forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well. But, in any event, you were a citizen of the SFRY, regardless of the fact or whether you knew the legislation regarding republican citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It would say, "Citizen of SFRY, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nationality, Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me now to ask you a few questions linked to the family and origins of Mr. Cerkez, because somehow I got the feeling that you are familiar with the family, or at least some of its members. Specifically, did you know the father of the accused Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The family of Mr. Mario Cerkez in Vitez was a decent family, a prominent family. I never heard anything bad about them. His father and mother worked in the post office. They were respected as employees. His wife worked with me in the same work organisation; not with me in a team, but she was working in the dental department. Occasionally, she worked in the general practice surgery. She's a really reliable person who worked well. There were never any criticisms against her. For a while, I was the director of the health centres, and before these events and conflicts, I never heard anything about Mario Cerkez or his wife or the other members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everyone knew his father in Vitez, because he worked on the maintenance of telephones and he would always be very helpful in dealing with all citizens. It was really a respectable family in Vitez, and people respected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether ever, prompted by any kind of event, did you doubt or suspect that this family, as a whole, or any member of that family might have any kind of ethnic prejudices?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that Mario Cerkez's mother worked in the post office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was she dealing with the general public at the counter or in the offices?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His mother was Ivanka. She worked at the counter with customers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have to slow down because of the interpretation. If I tell you that a witness claimed, a couple of days ago, that Mrs. Ivanka worked as a cashier in a shop, and you just said she worked at the post office counter, --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was an office the employees were working behind, and I know that Ivanka worked at the counter occasionally in this office. On one occasion, she asked me -- she had some medical problems, and she asked when she could come for an examination. She's a very nice woman, and I never heard that she had any -- that there was any unpleasantness on her part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you're sure she worked in the post office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you knew Mario Cerkez from the SDS, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kovacic, we're having the same problem, especially with translation. Could you slow down a bit and wait between question and answer? It's going to make life easier for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How close were you at work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was head of the medical service or the occupational medicine department of chemical organisations of UNIS. The colleagues working with Mario Cerkez would often invite me for a cup of coffee, and Mario Cerkez would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that at work, you knew him quite well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Once a year, I had to make an inventory of medical supplies, of which the gentleman was in charge, and we knew each other well. There were no problems between us. Mario Cerkez was on good terms also with my wife, who was a graduate economist employed in the SPS factory as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of those encounters and this good knowledge of Mr. Cerkez, you can say that he had no negative ethnic views or bias before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, also linked to the employment of Mr. Cerkez, he also had friendly relations and relations at work with the mentioned Sefkija Dzidic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think Sefkija Dzidic was his superior from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the SPS, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were on good terms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think they were on good terms, as far as I know. As far as I know Mario Cerkez from before the war, I am not aware of him being in conflict with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Cerkez socialised with Mr. Djidic even outside work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's quite possible. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was precisely Mr. Cerkez's job at SPS? What is it that he did, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez was in charge of equipment. He was also in charge of a field vehicle, and he also mentioned that -- there were medical supplies there, and once I saw lots of sports equipment there, and as I worked for the football club, Mario Cerkez asked me, "Well, does your club need this," and gave me some 20 pairs of something for children who were being coached at the football club. So that was his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And those stocks that you spoke about, all this equipment, all this stock, this was equipment and perhaps all that would be needed by the plant in case of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How would you rank that particular job? Was he a superior or was he a clerk? What would you say he would be on the hierarchical ladder, what role he would have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. He was a responsible clerk for that particular kind of work, but he was not a manager. I just don't know what one would call that particular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At any rate, he was not a manager?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that the SDA and the HDZ were the parties which shared in the power, or rather they divided various offices between themselves after the elections of 1990. You mentioned, by way of illustrating that particular point, that Mr. Santic was the mayor of the municipality, that Mr. Fuad Kaknjo was the president of the executive board of the municipality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these two offices -- that is, these two posts -- are the two most important political offices in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Also, on the basis of the agreement reached by these two parties, were all the other officers of relevance distributed in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you then remember, perhaps, for instance, head of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Muslim from Vitez who had lived in Vitez for a long time, even though he was not born in Vitez, and his name was Hakija Cengic. So he was the head of the TO on the basis of the understanding between the two parties. That was the commander of the Territorial Defence; that was the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember about the finance? Who held the treasury?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The finances were the responsibility of the executive board, so Fuad Kaknjo, the president of the executive board, I believe; Dragan Rados, a lawyer, was responsible for business; then an economist, and that property was managed by Midhat Varupa, who was a Muslim; and then Defence affairs were run by Stipo Krizanac. I knew all those people very well, because they all came from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, on the basis of what you have just said, could one say that the officers in the municipal authority were evenly distributed, evenly divided between Croats and Muslims, by ethnic standards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not take part in this, but yes, I do think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it -- of course, as far as you know -- was it at considerable variance with the situation before the elections, that is, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, people were brought to take up some affairs at the recommendation of the municipal committees, and this was one of the principal conditions, that a person needed to have a recommendation, a reference of the municipal committee, at any rate, some high-ranking officers. In this particular case there were democratic elections, and those people were truly and generally elected to these executive offices, but the municipal assembly needed to confirm these appointments as proposed by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, we know what we are talking about, but other people may not be conversant with all this. So you said on the basis of the references of the committee, so what committee? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the committee played a decisive role -- perhaps not only the decisive, but played a very important role when it came to appointments and elections of various officials in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only their municipality; in business as well. People needed -- how to put it -- a green light of the municipal League of Communists committee. They needed this reference before the Workers' Council would confirm the appointment. Without it, nobody could be appointed to any important office, be it in politics or business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. And after the war, you said this was based on the agreement of parties, so in other words, politics was involved still?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, has anything of consequence -- has there been any change of consequence? Before, there was a committee, and now it's an understanding between parties, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All offices were agreed by the parties. Well, perhaps the manner in which people are appointed has changed. In Vitez, for instance, we all cast our ballots and voted for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me -- I mean, this is politically interesting, and a novel time, in political terms. Did Mario Cerkez in any way, in any manner whatsoever, participate in election campaigns, in the elections? Was he elected to an office? Did he ever appear as a person who would be politically active?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know, since I did not appear -- I was put on the list. I told them not to do it, but they did put me on, I figured somewhere midway down the list. I just said that I wasn't active in politics ever, nor am I today, and I simply did not like it, so I don't know about Mario Cerkez. In 1990, I did not take part, so I really do not know what he was active in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you figured on one of the lists, and there were quite a number of them; you would have noticed if Cerkez had been on one of those lists?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite frankly, at that time, I did not -- I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Could you tell us, please, but very briefly, in two or three sentences, what you thought about the SDA at that time; that is, on the eve of the elections or at the time of the elections. What I mean is the educational structure of the SDA, so educational structure, please, will you confine yourself to that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The SDA in Vitez included some intellectuals, but there were many more Vitez intellectuals in parties like SDP or the Reformist Party. Then the Democratic Alliance of Socialist Youth also involved a number of Muslim intellectuals. I should say that a majority of Vitez intellectuals of Muslim origin adopted and joined those parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But could one say, even if speaking in very rough terms, could one really say that the SDA was a populist party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really could not say. All I can say is that it was people from rural areas who voted for the SDA in large numbers. Whether that would describe it as "populist" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. So we can accept, and without fearing any misunderstanding between us, that in terms of the educational -- of the professional structure of the membership, it was perhaps below the SDP and some other parties that you mentioned? I know it is very difficult to say. I'm referring to the feeling.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you know, we had some very prominent Muslims in Vitez: Engineers, physicians, dentists, and others, who were members of non-nationalistic parties. In the executive board and in the city board, in the town board, there were also some intellectuals from Vitez, but the intellectual composition, I think it was much -- it was stronger, and by far, in the Reformist Party of Ante Markovic, or of the SDP. I think that they had much more intellectual weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the HDZ as regards the educational structure? Could it be likened to the one in the SDA, or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Vitez, about 60 per cent of the Muslims -- I mean in the municipality -- voted for the SDA. Also a very high percentage of Croats voted for the HDZ, a very high percentage, very, very high. I mean over 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the HDZ, then, won an overwhelming majority of Croat votes in the elections of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the SDA did not win so many votes, or rather that high percentage of votes, of Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I was told by those who were running those affairs at the time, I know that around 60 per cent of Muslims voted for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, does it mean that Bosniak Muslims, as a constituency, as a body of voters, also opted for other parties and not only for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we now address the crisis staff that you spoke about. You said that as far as you could remember, the crisis staff began to operate sometime in February and March 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said, if I understood you properly, that the crisis staff was set up at the proposal of the HDZ; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at the executive board of the Vitez SDA, professor Munib Kajmovic, president of the executive board, and the president of the executive board of Vitez, Fuad Kaknjo, said that HDZ representatives were proposing to set up the crisis staff as a body which would take over the mandate of the assembly, as there were very many problems and they were in immediate danger of war. So they explained that that body would be more operative, more efficient, that it would be less members, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. We don't need to go into detail. Tell me, Doctor, this is the beginning, or, say, the spring of 1992: What danger of war are we talking about at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the territory, we had -- first of all in Croatia, '91, the political situation was highly precarious. In spring, that is, in the former half of 1992, we already had some incursions from Montenegro and Serbia of the Territorial Defence. I can't remember the date, but the villages of Ravno, then Bijelina, then roadblocks in Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into all this detail, and try to be more expedient. So is it correct that at that time the JNA aggression supported by Serbs -- that is local Serbs, in Bosna -- was quite evident, was plainly evident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was expected in view of the way things were developing, and the republican assemblies could not agree with regard to the status of republics, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So these two principal parties in Vitez now suggested that rather than the municipal assembly, which worked in peacetime, a crisis staff should be set up as a tool, as -- don't interrupt me, please -- as an instrument of government which would be suited to the period of when war threatened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a proposal of HDZ representatives, as far as I can remember, at the executive board of the SDA, Midhat Varupa, who was a member of the executive board, said that it was not in conformity with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that we should seek instructions from the top and that we should perhaps set up a war presidency. But with good relations in mind, we nevertheless voted for this HDZ proposal, yet saying that it had to be verified by the municipal assembly, confirmed there, because it was taking over the jurisdiction of the municipal assembly. It had to be approved by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And so the crisis staff, as a matter of fact, did take over the functions of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at that time, or about that time, there was the notorious incident -- and I believe we all saw it on television -- when Alija Izetbegovic was arrested at the Sarajevo airport after his return from some negotiations abroad, and it was the JNA which arrested him. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Are we referring to that particular time? Excuse me, is that that particular time that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think we did it a little bit before that, but to the best of my recollection, it was sometime towards the end of March, or perhaps early April, I mean, Alija Izetbegovic's arrest at the Sarajevo airport in '92. We saw it on television. The Sarajevo television transmitted those events.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I believe it was sometime in April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as a citizen, as an educated citizen, you were involved in politics; now, was there any dilemma, was there any doubt who was the aggressor and who was attacking Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, in Vitez, we thought above all that -- I should say an overwhelming majority of the population -- that there was an aggression against Croatia, and it was anticipating the aggression against Bosnia, and it was the JNA, or rather the -- and an overwhelming majority of the population thought so, since there were very few Serbs in our case, only about four or five per cent, I think, and they also thought that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was it the first time that in the municipality of Vitez you felt, you sensed that this JNA aggression and the local Serb aggression, rather Bosnian Serb aggression, had reached your threshold, that it was no longer something abstract?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned those events in Herzegovina, the television broadcast, then the events in Bijelina, and it all pointed at this, that situation in the Bosnian Krajina and in West Bosnia. It was precisely because of that that we agreed and decided to do all within our power to forestall a conflict in Vitez and to try to raise the combat preparedness of people, of militarily-aged men, to be organised and to take part in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understood you. "To forestall the conflict in Vitez": What conflict are we referring to at that time? This is the former half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Vitez, I said that there were very few Serbs, there was a village called Tolovici not far from Vitez, and that was where first incidents started, or at least that was how it was represented to us. The village Preocica, which was a Muslim village, and the village of Tolovici, which was a mixed village, two-thirds Serb and one-third Muslim. The former army left very many weapons with the Serb residents of that village. And in Vitez, from the police -- later on the reserve police also received weapons and in the SPS security, SPS factory, security in Vitez, we did not have any weapons. So this gave rise to a major concern amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it why from Preocica pressure was brought to bare on Tolovici and the Serbs practically left the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know what it is about. That was presented as a problem in Vitez. The vice-president of the municipality was a Serb, Mijatovic, and, Slobodan, his deputy and a lawyer, were invited to the crisis staff and the crisis staff concluded -- we concluded at the crisis staff that Serbs in Vitez needed protection. The chief of the police in Vitez, Pero Skopljak, was made responsible for that and the police commander Mahmud Sabanvic was also made responsible for this and Tomo Hrustanovic, as the president of the neighbourhood community, he was a civilian policeman in Vitez, and Munib Kajmovic, president of the SDA party in Vitez, were asked to go to that village, talk to people there, and to conduct an investigation as to who was causing trouble, who was starting trouble there, because meanwhile a Serb had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Cvijan Mijatovic. He was my schoolfellow in the elementary school. We asked that the investigation be conducted into that case to see who had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Has ever the answer been provided by investigation? Has investigation reached a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbs left the area? Regardless of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On one occasion, Pero Skopljak, the chief of the police, came to the meeting of the crisis staff, came with a list there. I think it was June. I don't know, I can't -- and said at the crisis staff meeting that the Serb residents of the village of Tolovici were placing themselves under the HVO protection, and he brought a list, since they had turned over their weapons. If I remember properly it was matter of 120 rifles. There were also two recoilless guns on that list, if I remember well. He showed us that particular list, and he said there would be no more problems and that they were now placed under the protection of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And otherwise the village of Tolovici, as you said, had a Serb majority population, and the rest were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that two-thirds of the population were Serbs and one-third were Muslims. As a physician I often went to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there were no Croats in that village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did similar things happen in the village of Trnopolje, in the village of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These are villages in a row; it is a cluster of villages. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. They are hamlets, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we are referring to one and the same area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was the same situation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Grabak, Hrasnice, Crnovlje, a bit higher up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, those -- there were Serbs, too. Less of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was the only part of the municipality with where you could find a larger concentration of the Serb population; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and in the urban part of Vitez, but those were mostly Serb intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But when we're talking about villages, this was the only concentration?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was yet another small village where Serbs and Croats lived. I think its name was Zaselje, I believe so, yes, the village of Zaselje, where Serbs and Croats lived, mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Kovacic, it's now time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is perfectly okay with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will keep an eye on the clock, won't you, during this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Before we adjourn, there is a question I want to ask of the witness, please: Dr. Mujezinovic, you were giving evidence yesterday about the refugees who came into the municipality, and you said that in 1991, refugees started to arrive from Croatia. You then said that in September and October, Muslim refugees arrived, and you remember you said they stayed with relatives or went to summer cottages, and you said there were about 4.000. What I wanted to know, and while it's in my mind, I'd be grateful if you'd deal with it, is this: Which year did the Muslim refugees start arriving in September and October? Was it 1991, or was it another year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 1992, the latter half of 1992 is when they began to arrive, first from East Bosnia and then from West Bosnia. Muslims, and a large wave of Croat refugees and Muslim refugees from Jajce, arrived in November. I don't know how many were they, but what I heard was that Croat refugees alone were some thousand strong. But after that, quite a number of them left Vitez. Some of them stayed for a while. Some came for check-ups to me, and they wanted to go to Croatia, they wanted to go to Tomislavgrad, and I think that very few stayed back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us round off this part about the Serbs in the villages we've mentioned. Two minor details. There was a group of Serbs in the hamlet near Kruscica, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they did not leave, they were not exiled, they stayed on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, a part of them left and a part of them stayed behind. I don't know how many stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything to the effect that these inhabitants of Tolovici, the Serbs of Tolovici, having formed something called the SVO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to tender a few documents containing conclusions of meetings of the crisis staff. If I may, I would suggest that we admit them into evidence as a single document, though there are five or six of them. Then we could number them A, B, C, D, because this would speed up the proceedings. I have only a few questions related to these documents. They have all been translated, and I'm glad to be able to inform Judge Bennouna that we even have a French translation, thanks to the Registry. Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please? The documents are in order. First comes the document in the B/S/C language, and then the English and Croatian translations have been attached. No, I beg your pardon, English and French translations. Each of these Croatian documents is marked by hand with a number in the right-hand corner, starting with "678", so as to speed up and facilitate communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll ask the Registry for a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D12/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would ask you to separate the documents. (In English) Separate the translations. Could you please put all the B/S/C languages in a row as a bundle? You may just take out the translations. Yes, okay. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Put the English version on the ELMO. Okay. (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you managed to look through the first document marked with the number "6"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So these are conclusions from a meeting of the crisis staff, held on the 24th of April, 1992. I should like to draw your attention to point 5. It emanates from this point that you and your colleague, Dr. Zvonko Kajic, were authorised by the crisis staff to exempt, fully or partially, from military obligations all sick citizens of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already stated that earlier, that I was in charge of this. Dr. Kajic is a Croat from Vitez who had only just come to Vitez. He was a military doctor in the former JNA. I think that he had just reported to us, telling us that he had abandoned the former JNA, and he came to work in our medical centre. As he had this military experience, I was advised to cooperate with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless you want to know about Dr. Kajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a simple question. (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, without further elaboration, will you answer the following question for me? Was this an important authorisation that you had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was a very important one, especially in times of war, of course. On the 24th of April, 1992, there was no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean no threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a threat of war, but there was no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The next document, marked with the number "7" in the right-hand corner, a meeting of the crisis committee held on the 4th of May, 1992. Let me draw your attention to point 1. Here you have been asked, together with Dr. Tibold, to analyse the widespread disease among children in Vitez. Did you work on that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. Franjo Tibold is an epidemiologist, and in view of the fact that I was in charge of these things, as necessary I would engage other doctors, in this case an epidemiologist, so that we should study the causes of the emergence of this disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you work on that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But afterall, that was seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Under point 7, mention is made here, "On report of fulfilment of work obligations." What is that, a work obligation? Could you explain that to the Court, but as briefly as possible?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those days in Vitez, work organisations were requested to lend their workers to the HVO and the Territorial Defence. That was requested of them, and work organisations submitted lists of workers, especially from the military industry, that they couldn't do without. Then we would call up the managers of those enterprises, of those companies, to see who was essential among those workers for the process of production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that each citizen, in accordance with the regulations in force at the time, was given certain assignments either in the military, as a soldier, or at his place of work in those enterprises which were of vital importance for the population and the military?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In those days, every able-bodied citizen of Vitez who was a military conscript had to be assigned somewhere. Either he had a work obligation or he was a member of one of the military units in Vitez. But those military units had to give lists of names of people in their units to the work organisations in which they were employed so they knew where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding this assignment of people to work obligations and to the military, was there any body in charge of this within the civilian authorities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the highest-level body in the municipality was the crisis staff, so it was the crisis staff that was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could a unit, a military unit itself, recruit a person, as that unit doesn't know whether that person had a work obligation or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those days, we had a Secretariat of Defence, and all these needs were met through the municipal Secretariat for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were these activities carried on later by the Defence Department when the HVO government was established?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you ever assigned to a work obligation as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said several times that my work obligation was to work in the crisis staff and to form the medical service under extraordinary conditions. But I also worked in the medical centre as a practising physician, and I also went to Travnik on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you could not be called up by the military as a soldier, because your work obligation was to work as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But it was my obligation to treat all citizens, including the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we go on, then? The document marked with the number "8" has to do with the 12th of May, 1992. This was tendered into evidence by the Prosecutor yesterday. Let me just note that as you said yesterday, you were asked to give a certain quantity of antibiotics to the Vitez Health Centre. Let's go on to the next document, number 9, adopted a couple of days later on the 15th of May. Under point 2, we see more or less the same conclusion, noting that this continues to be your assignment. Does that mean that it wasn't carried out and it was urgent? Of course, if you can still remember.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In work organisations, the SPS and Vitezit, we had quite a good medical infirmary, and these supplies were taken from those dispensaries. A part was given to the health centre in the town itself and another part to the Ribnjak Motel in Kruscica. Acting pursuant to these conclusions, this is what I did, because this was agreed by Dr. Bruno Buzuk as well because there was quite a lot of medical supplies available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But tell us, Doctor, were they only antibiotics or were other supplies involved?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Because this was a specific factory producing gunpowder, there were frequent incidents, there were explosions, and the workers would have very large burns. There were special sheets and bandages to bandage bodies. And I think this is an error, because what should have been said was military medical supplies that we had in the factories available in the case of such major injuries when there were explosions in the factory plants, by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, do I understand you correctly, these were supplies necessary for the protection of civilians in the case of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was military medical supplies, mostly. Supplies that were mostly used by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next document, marked with a number "10" in the right-hand corner. These are conclusions of an extraordinary session of the crisis staff held on the 22nd of May which you mentioned yesterday. You told us about that session, that it was convened in the middle of the night and so on. You told us what your role was. Could you please look through the document very briefly and tell us, does it relate to the event that you described yesterday? Doctor, is this the meeting that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I got as far as Point 2. Sefkjia Dzidic is a mistake. It was Kaknjo Fuad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is an error naming Sefkija Dzidic, in your opinion. But on the whole, does this document correspond to the meeting you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. But this was written on the 22nd of May, and I said that this occurred in the night between the 20th and the 21st, and we were called to attend the meeting of the crisis staff. So allow me to read it through. Yes, that is that document, and the document doesn't mention who was present. I was saying yesterday that it wasn't Sefkjia who attended the meeting but Hakija Cengic. I don't remember that Sefkjia was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let me now ask you, having mentioned this event which prompted the meeting, in the examination-in-chief yesterday, you said that Cerkez appeared to you to be drunk, under the influence of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that he seemed to be under the influence of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. How were you sitting in relation to Cerkez? How far were you from Cerkez? Were you sitting round a big table? Of course, as far as you can remember, because this was a long time ago. Just tell us what you remember about this event.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the office of the president of the municipal assembly there was a long desk, there was one for the chair, and as far as I can remember, I think I sat across him at the desk, across the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it's not a big room, after all, so it was only the breadth of the table which separated you from Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know whether he was sitting at that round table. I mean, there was one oblong table and one round desk, one round table, if I can remember, really, what his office looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understand it's very difficult to be accurate, but how far were you from Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we were together at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you how far away were you from him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was far enough or close enough to hear what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you had an opportunity of seeing him well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I listened to what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Please, as a physician, could you tell me, what are the symptoms, generally recognised symptoms, of drunkenness?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a physician, a man who has taken in a largish quantity of alcohol is usually red in the face, very relaxed, speaks in a loud voice. Some people are aggressive, some are not. These would be some general signs. Some tend to sing. To put it simply, small doses of alcohol will help one to relax, and larger quantities have the opposite effect.
